source.title: Generalization Measures for Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Transfer
source.authors: Saksham Bassi; Duygu Ataman; Kyunghyun Cho

record.tranche_reason: Tests how generalization measures and sharpness-based optimization relate to zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, a new language-model setting beyond the claim versions' stated image-classification and standard-training settings.
record.gate_note: Reports test-accuracy correlations with margin, two sharpness measures, and Frobenius distance, plus accuracy comparisons across fine-tuning objectives. These results concern cross-lingual transfer and its measures; they do not test memorization of random labels, width past interpolation, CNN versus fully connected image classifiers, optimizer comparisons under the versioned tuning conditions, batch size, dropout, or example removal.
record.test_reason: The study measures correlations with zero-shot cross-lingual accuracy, not the train–test generalization gap named in V7. Its difference-based sharpness and modified alpha-based measure do not establish the magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance or ranking comparison V7 specifies. No other version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors conclude that margin and their proposed difference-based sharpness correlate with zero-shot cross-lingual performance. They report objective-dependent relationships, no strong direct overall relationship for Frobenius distance, and unstable alpha-based sharpness with weak relationships for baseline and SAM. These are accuracy correlations, not measurements of train–test gaps or causal evidence that flatness improves transfer.
record.recipe_differences: Fine-tunes pretrained multilingual language models on English NLI and measures transfer accuracy and correlations with margin, sharpness, and parameter distance; the claim versions concern other tasks and interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported relationship between measures and test performance depends on the optimization objective used during fine-tuning; the authors also report unstable alpha-based sharpness computation and heuristic noise-scale choices.

fits_no_version.finding: On XNLI, baseline mBERT has margin–accuracy correlation 0.801 and difference-based sharpness–accuracy correlation -0.845. Table 1 separately reports positive margin and negative sharpness correlations for MVR, SAM, FIM and mT5.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Margin and difference-based sharpness correlate with cross-lingual accuracy within the tested models and objectives.

fits_no_version.finding: Modified alpha-based sharpness correlations with XNLI accuracy are 0.249, -0.471, -0.166 and -0.440 for baseline, MVR, SAM and FIM. The computation can terminate at extreme radius values.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: This implementation of alpha-based sharpness is unstable and does not consistently track cross-lingual accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: On PAWS-X, margin–accuracy correlations are 0.998, 0.997 and 0.995; difference-based sharpness correlations are -0.289, -0.708 and -0.622.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Margin strongly tracks cross-lingual PAWS-X accuracy in the tested models, while sharpness correlations vary by model.

fits_no_version.finding: Across repeated runs, SAM generally achieves the best average zero-shot accuracy; FIM performs comparatively poorly but has the greatest stability.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning objectives differ in average cross-lingual accuracy and variability across seeds.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors find no strong direct overall relationship between Frobenius distance from initialization and accuracy, despite FIM combining high distance with poor performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Distance from initialization does not strongly track cross-lingual accuracy in these experiments.

record.problems: The paper reports correlations rather than evidence about the train-test error gap; the main XNLI correlations aggregate across methods and languages, and the PAWS-X sharpness coefficients are not interpreted individually in text. The proposed sharpness algorithm still requires heuristic tuning of noise scale and projection coefficient. Alpha-based sharpness can yield extreme values and fails to show a strong relationship for Baseline and SAM.
record.rows_left_out: No separately quantified language-wise measurements were extracted from Figures 3 and 4 because the supplied text gives no values and these plots are not described with separately stated numbers. Figure 5's Frobenius-distance scatter values are figure-only; the textual aggregate/model-specific statement is recorded in R15. No result is reported for V1–V8 as framed.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label held-out generalization under the same architecture and recipe.
Width-dependent test error beyond zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimization under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance versus train–test gaps among similarly fitted convolutional networks, and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Table 1 contains separate correlations for each objective, contrary to R1–R2's aggregation description. Its additional coefficients do not warrant version-specific missing entries because they test none of V1–V8.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width beyond interpolation in one-hidden-layer ReLU networks.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer generalization under the stated benchmark and tuning conditions.
Large versus small batch training and epoch-budget effects.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its ranking of gaps among networks with similarly low training loss.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.
